utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith and Selma Sakic for the Prosecution. Sorry. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of the Stanisic Defence team, Slobodan Cvijetic, Tatjana Savic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Daniella Sinobad appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I remind witness, before Ms. Korner resumes her examination-in-chief, that he's still on his oath. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, I regret that I want to go back and read the transcript over night to ask you about just one matter in respect again of the bunker that you spoke about yesterday that was in Vogosca. You told the Court that you saw -- you realised that people were being held there apart from being told that, because you saw people walking round the bunker coming out. "They told us they were living in the bunker." That's at page 15590. What people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I didn't know those people. I just saw a group of people in front of the entrance to the bunker. It was a nice day, and this was very close to this building where we were meeting. And also, nobody was trying to hide this. They told us these people were prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So the people you saw outside the bunker were prisoners.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you discover what ethnicity the prisoners were?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No, I did not discover, but we were told that these were Muslims -- or, rather, Bosniaks from the settlements around Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. And second matter, the people that you saw in the warehouse in -- in Ilijas, were they in uniform or were they in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I haven't seen anyone wearing a uniform. I cannot tell you things that are not true. They were all in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I want to move very quickly through, please, the rest of the matters I want to ask you about because we have a limited amount of time. If I could stop misplacing my note, we might get on a bit quicker. Ah. Right. Generally speaking, is this correct as you told us yesterday, that the MO -- the Ministry of Justice, the ministry, took over detention facilities from the end of July or beginning of August?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Penal and correctional institution. That's part of the Ministry of Justice was the institution that took over. And by the decision of the Presidency there was a reorganisation of the penal and correctional facilities, and Butmir where these people were inmates was also placed under this institution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about the date, please. Was that about the end of July, beginning of August?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: In late July. You can see from the notebook. The moment the police left Kula the security was taken over by the employees of the KP Dom Kula.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not just talking about Kula. I'm talking about all the other facilities, detention facilities, that you inspected or dealt with. Were they taken over by the ministry of justice at the end of July, beginning of August?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: In this case we're discussing only Kula. Only Kula was involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. We're going to look at some of the documents that you dealt with. We've already looked at some. Who was providing security for all the places in which people were being kept until July/August? Was it the Ministry of Justice or was it some other organisation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Workers of the Ministry of Justice were not securing anyone in any penal or correctional facility. I don't know about Foca, whether there was the army or the former employees of this facility. I cannot tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's -- perhaps we'll get at this quicker through some of the documents. Can you have a look, please, at document number P165 at tab 22. Right. Is that a report that you and a gentleman named Goran Saric made on yet another inspection of detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a report from Bileca that we drafted on the basis of a decision reached by the government to tour the area. We went to the barracks in Bileca, Trebinje, Gacko, and a pupils' home in Bileca and Gacko. We were told that there were no camps. Colonel Cigarac [phoen] in the barracks in Bileca -- should I slow down?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I'd like you to deal, please, just with my questions rather than volunteering information, because we've got, as I say, limited time. All I want to ask you about this report is to whom did you deliver that report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who did you deliver the report to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: To the minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In Bileca, you spoke to Mr. Vujovic, the head of the SJB there, and he told you that 140 Muslims were accommodated in their premises. Do you mean the SJB? By "their premises."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It was in the students dorm and these people who were isolated were secured by the police employees.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. These people apparently had committed, from your report, no crime but were being kept there for their own safety. That's what you recorded. That's what the police told you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. If I may provide a broader explanation in two sentences.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: At the time, the Neretva River valley, Mostar area, people were leaving that area. When I say "people," I mean the reserve of forces, paramilitaries and so on, and they all came to Bileca. Mr. Vujovic, who was the chief of the municipality, believed that many problems can come out of this situation, so they isolated the people and kept them in this students dorm. Women were being food for these people. And after I came -- it was the police that was providing security for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. All I'm concerned about is this: If as you reported the SJB was telling you these people were there for their own safety, why did you recommend that the people who were over 60 should be released? If you look at the end of the second paragraph -- third paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: When we went out, we received instructions that once we came to a camp, and we didn't know that we were going to find such a situation, people who were detained, prisoners of war who were detained, that there shouldn't be in detention people over 60 years of age, children, and women. That was the instruction I received then. That's how I acted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but these, according to your report as to what this SJB chief told you, these weren't prisoners at all. These were people being kept for their own safety. So why should you, in that case, recommend that the people over 60 should be released into the dangers of this particular area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It is possible that I drafted this just basing it according to the instruction and that maybe I haven't found any people who were over 60 or women or children. I didn't mean to suggest that anyone should be released, especially when I was told that -- what kind of threats they're facing, that the mosque in the town was destroyed, and that was done by the paramilitaries. I believe that what they did was a smart move.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Just read, would you, please, to yourself the last sentence of paragraph 3 in your report. Bottom of the page. Now, does that or does not that say --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I can see. It is possible that I said this. I don't know why. Probably just keeping to what I was given in the instruction. And you're right. Why would they be released in a situation like this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because can I put this to you, Mr. Avlijas, that you knew and the police knew that these people were being illegally held simply because they were Muslims. Isn't that why you made the recommendation at the end?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was a leading question. The witness is being told what to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I wouldn't have thought it was a leading question, Mr. Cvijetic, but did I think that it is -- struck me as something that should be reserved for submissions at the end. The report is there. The witness has been invited on three occasions to comment on it, and we have his answer. The rest is for inference and argument.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour's right to that extent, except I thought perhaps maybe just once the witness might like to tell us really what happened. All right. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So can we move now, please, to the next, which is a report, again I think from you -- sorry, it's document, please -- oh, sorry, before I leave that last document, can I just check something. No. Yes. Let's move to the next report, please, then. It's document 65 ter 2825, tab 25. If we go to the second page, just so we can see the signature. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To whom did you give this report? If we go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: To the Ministry of justice, the minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I see. I think it's rather an odd translation of the ministry of justice for some reason. Right. Was this a further inspection of various detention facilities, this time in the area of the autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. This is about a meeting of the representatives of the Banja Luka region from all various structures. Milan Trbojevic, Mr. Milan Trbojevic, vice-president or -- of the government, Dragan Kalinic who was minister of health, and I also think although I didn't mention in the report minister of defence Mr. Subotic attended. When we look at the attendees it would have been logical for Mr. Mandic, the minister to be present, but he sent me instead. I attended the meeting, and the topics listed here were discussed at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. You -- you -- what you say in this, that there were representatives of the army. Was that General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. General Gvero was not in attendance. I think it was one of the generals from the Krajina Corps who attended, or some of the high-ranking officer. I can't remember. It was a long time ago. I didn't write it down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Representatives of the internal affairs bodies. That's the police. Was Stojan Zupljanin there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zupljanin was there. Simo Drljaca as well. Basic and District prosecutors, president of the District and Basic Court, mayor of Banja Luka, the late Dr. Predrag Radic, Vukic, as far as I remember, and some other people attended. The hall was packed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. During the course of this meeting did the topic of the killings which had taken place in the area of Koricanske Stijene come up?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, and that resulted in a troublesome discussion initiated by late Mayor Radic who was very angry, who said that this throws bad light on the area of Banja Luka, and the army joined in. There was also present the chief of the SJB of Prijedor whose policemen committed the terrible crime. Then the members of the army told us about what the location looked like, that it was a cliff. They said also that they went to the site. Mr. Zupljanin said that he had formed a team, that the on-site investigation had been carried out, that a criminal report had been submitted, and if I'm not mistaken, I think Mr. Puvacic who was the Basic prosecutor was asked to speak. He was asked how far have they come with the investigation, but the conclusion was that this whole situation had to be fully cleared up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. You say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Korner. There's something which is wrongly translated. It's at page 9, line 24. Can the witness be asked to repeat last sentence. It was recorded. Mr. Puvacic who was the Basic prosecutor was asked to it speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honours give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I'm told there's agreement about this, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, could you repeat your sentence in respect of what you said about Mr. Puvacic, the prosecutor, because we think there's a wrong translation.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Mr. Stojan Zupljanin informed those present that the on-site investigation had been carried out at Koricanske Stijene, that CSB Banja Luka team went there, that they drafted a criminal report. Now, I cannot remember whether it included the names of the perpetrators or whether it was an unknown perpetrator report, and that this report was submitted to Mr. Puvacic, the Basic prosecutor. So they turned to Mr. Puvacic and asked him what has been done until that moment about this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you -- you said that -- well, actually, I suppose I ought to stick to that for a moment. What did Mr. Puvacic say in reply?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: That investigation was ongoing. A standard reply that the procedure is underway, and that allegedly they had problems because the perpetrators were at large somewhere. To the best of my recollection. I do have some recollection of it, because this was a rather heavy case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was it Mr. Puvacic who said that the perpetrators were at large? Did Mr. Drljaca say anything about the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It was a difficult situation, because these were employees of the Prijedor SJB. I -- this is not my field of expertise, and I can't discuss this much, but I had this feeling that the whole meeting was looking at Mr. Drljaca. He was supposed to tell why. I think Drljaca may have said that he had tried to arrest the perpetrators and that one or two of them were at large, that they fled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But nobody at that meeting, from what you say, was in any doubt that the people who had committed this crime were police officers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No, there was no doubt about that. That was clearly stated. Not at any time there was any doubt about someone else being involved and not the policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Did Mr. Zupljanin say anything to Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I do think there was some conflict between the two of them on one occasion during the meeting, because one was saying, "These are your policemen. It's impossible that they've just fled." I know that Simo Drljaca wasn't really humble at the time. I can't remember his response, but the whole situation was very charged.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this document be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit -- as Exhibit P1635, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we now move, please, to your major report, which is already an exhibit. It's at tab 29. P393. Thank you. Right. I know that you're very familiar with this report, Mr. Avlijas, as indeed I think are the Chamber now. 27th of October. Whose signature is that on the front page of the letter to the Presidency and the various officials?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Of Minister Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This was your report, though, to Mr. Mandic. Was it Mr. Mandic who had instructed you to carry out this inspection?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. At a meeting one day prior to the time I went out to do a tour, I think it was based on some instruction by the government, I was told to tour all the locations around Prijedor. You cannot find it written in there, but I think there was some pressure after a meeting in Geneva where representative I think maybe of the Red Cross, Sadako Ogata, who at that meeting in Geneva had said that there was some terrible things happening on the ground, that Trnopolje camp was re-established, and I was tasked to tour a number of places and draft a report about my tour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want to deal with a few matters in this report. When you went to Vlasenica, you started -- can we go, sorry, to the next page in both English and B/C/S. You started your report by saying: "According to information from the IRC, there is allegedly a collection camp at this location, in the immediate vicinity of the town, in a place called Luke." Do you now know what that camp was actually called?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I later found out it was called Susica, but I wasn't sure then whether I've confused the terms Luke and Susica. And during the proofing and also during the interviews, I asked to be shown air photos, and, yes, that's the camp. I toured this camp, and what you can see here, I could say that, yes, that was Susica based on the lay out of the terrain and the facilities there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if there's any dispute about this I'll show the witness the photographs but it takes up time to look at. Is there any dispute about what he actually saw was Susica, because if so, I'll get him to identify the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not a contentious issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And in the context of time, you have ten minutes remaining, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know. That's why I'm speeding up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you also -- can I just deal with one matter. Yes. You talked about Prijedor in item 4. That's in the -- sorry, the one, two -- fourth page in English and the third page in B/C/S. And -- actually, I think we need to go, sorry, to the next page in the B/C/S, because the part I want to refer to ... There. You talk about in the second paragraph of your report on Prijedor that there was a meeting at Prijedor during the course of your inspection with the representatives of the International Red Cross and other people. I just want to put to you and see if you can remember this. Was one of the other people there Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Stakic was, then the late Dr. Kovacevic, the late Simo Drljaca. Simo Srdac [phoen] who was the president of the Red Cross and a deputy in the RS Assembly, and I believe the SDS president there -- was there. On our behalf there was a Dr. Aleksic who was assistant minister of health, and Mr. Beat or Beat, I believe, who was also in attendance from the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, I think we'll discover that's Dr. Beat Schweizer. And was there, in fact, also present a representative of the -- the local newspaper "Kozarski Vjesnik"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I think there was a journalist there. Later on I found out that an article was published.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you read the article at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I did not. It was shown it me later, and I don't think it accurately reflects the truth of the matter, but that's my personal view.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Next can we quickly move to Sanski Most, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Next page in English. Same page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What you record in your report was "the information there is a camp in Sanski Most is not correct. In that area only four people were taken prisoner and transferred to the Manjaca camp ..." Who gave you the information that only four people had been taken prisoner during the course of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: A security officer. I contacted them for the most part whenever there was a danger in terms of access due to combat. They provided me such information, for example, for Sanski Most and Kotor Varos, I believe, because I don't go there myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who do you mean by a security officer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: From the Banja Luka Corps. Those who were in charge of that particular area. The Krajina Corps, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are you saying that you never met anybody in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No, I never met anybody in Sanski Most or in Kotor Varos, because I think there is a reference to Kotor Varos as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So you never made any attempt to -- to query or see whether the security officer was telling you the truth?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: There was no reason for me to disbelieve him. I had no time, and I really couldn't move about. Hence, I couldn't go out on my own in those areas where there were -- there was combat. I took his word for it, especially because he said that all of those taken prisoner were transferred to Manjaca. Later on we had a meeting in Banja Luka in August where it was said that all persons from the area of Krajina were located at Manjaca, and this is what I based my conclusion on and I trusted what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This report was after the Banja Luka meeting in August, but anyhow can we move very quickly finally to Ilidza and Hadzici. That's in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, Ms. Korner, there is -- again it is problem with this translation. The word "later" starts with -- doesn't appear from his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You did go, however, to Ilidza, didn't you, and Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you saw -- and you described in your report that there was a makeshift prison for prisoners of war Ilidza, which is organised, supervised by the public security station. It's in the secondary school in Ilidza. And also there was a sports facility at Hadzici, also with security being provided by the SJB there. Were you allowed by the police to inspect either of those two premises?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Let's start with Hadzici. In Hadzici, there were Bosniak prisoners who had been taken prisoner back in May 1992 by the army. They were transferred to Kula where they stayed until September or October 1992, when an all-for-all exchange was exchanged between -- for the camps at Tarcin and Kula.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. Can we -- I'm sorry, I don't think we've got it up on the screen, actually, which may be why you're going off like this. Can we have the next page, I think, in English. No. Ten is on the screen. No. All right. Go back, please. Yes -- no, that's it. Hadzici. Look, you said in your report that 90 people are accommodated in the Hadzici sports centre. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe the witness should be allowed to complete his sentence, and I believe he may even provide an answer to the question Ms. Korner was about to put.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The witness is talking about people who were transferred to Kula until September. I'm asking him about the 90 prisoners of war that he records in his -- in his report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, are you saying these are one and the same people, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: That is precisely what I wanted to say. These were the same people, because the exchange failed, because they couldn't be transferred elsewhere. The easiest thing was to move them to Hadzici. The group who -- that was in charge of it didn't do their job properly. They returned them to Hadzici, and they wanted to basically use these people as leverage to secure an exchange with Tarcin. They were secured by the workers of the police. The conditions were very bad, and those in charge of guarding them could hardly wait for the people to leave. Those people had been viciously mistreated back in June in Hadzici by paramilitaries. A lot of my friends were arrested who told me about all of that that had taken place at Kula. That is the same group.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You're -- you're saying this is the same group that were arrested in May, transferred to Kula, whenever it was. When did they get beaten up by paramilitaries in June then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Not in June, in May. In May. Before they were transferred to Kula they had gone through horrific torture by paramilitaries in Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. So you saw these people in October in Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. Those same people who were returned to Hadzici are the people I saw when they were in June and July at Kula. They could move freely about. Since I had lived in Hadzici for 17 years, I had a lot of really good friends who were detained there. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: -- asked the people who stood guard there to it allow me to see some of my friends and then those friends told me all about the mistreatment and torture.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They told you all about their mistreatment and torture where?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: In the gym when they were arrested in May, before their transfer to Kula.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And these are totally different from the -- the people from Hadzici that you spoke to when you were in Ilijas all those months ago -- or, rather, the same people.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Ilijas is a separate story. I was there on official business, and that's why people knew me there. As for Hadzici, I had lived there for 17 years. I was the court president there for eight years, and I was the secretary of the health centre there for a number of years. I had lots of friends there who found themselves in this misfortunate situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we now try and get some order into this. The people from Hadzici that you spoke to when you were there in Ilijas in June are --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Not in Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday, sir, you spoke to people from Hadzici who you knew when you were there in June. Now, are these people, the 90 prisoners of war described in your report, a different group? That's all I want. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. Ilijas is a separate group of people, and in Hadzici there was a different group of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you on this occasion in October allowed by the police to see these people in Hadzici? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: The regular policemen couldn't stand me, and the police commander had to intervene for me to be allowed to visit those people and see what the situation was, and the conditions were not met. They did not meet the standards required by the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Were you allowed in Ilidza to enter the secondary school which was being guarded by the police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: At Ilidza, I was not lucky enough to enter. They were guarded by some policemen who did not grant me access. And I asked to see those senior to them, but none of them were to be found in the police station. I only knew that there was a high school there, that there was a single toilet and a number of classrooms, and that these were not the conditions in which prisoners should be held. I used that as the basis of my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And finally in the conclusion to your report, you said: "In the cases --" Can we look at the -- yes, the last page in B/C/S, please. "In the cases of Zvornik, Hadzici, and Ilidza, we see that the Public Security Stations keep people in custody without any authorisation or justification in law because they have the authority to keep people in custody for no longer than three days." That was your opinion, was it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I followed common sense and the law. If the minister of the interior is included or a police station, the Law on Criminal Procedure prescribes the authority of the police and limits it to being able to hold someone in custody for three days. Whether there were any other conditions in place, that is something I didn't go into, but I'm simply sharing my view with you as a legal professional.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As a result of that -- actually, I think this is already an exhibit, so I don't need to show you that. Yes. Finally -- all right. Now, finally, Mr. Avlijas, in the places that you visited of detention during this period between the end of May and October 1992, who was providing the security for the detainees?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It depended on the location. Somewhere it was the army, and elsewhere it was the police. In Zvornik, when I visited, by sheer circumstance it was the police who had to secure some 40-plus prisoners, because they had simply been given these people by the army. They came from a number of different reception centres and held together. In Hadzici it was the police, in Ilidza the police, in Bileca the police, because it's all in my report. I can't deny that. As for the reasons for it, that is something I cannot provide you with an answer to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. And even before the place -- the other places that you visited and described to the Court, namely in Ilidza, in Ilija -- sorry, in Ilijas, in Vogosca, and other places, on each occasion was it the police who were providing the security?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I think there was a combination of the police and army. In Vogosca it was Brano Vlaco who had been a policeman before the war. Everyone knew that. And it was logical for me to conclude that the police stood guard there. In Ilijas I think it was the army, although I'm not certain. In Vogosca it was Brano Vlaco. That is certain. He was at the meeting, and we already ascertained that he was a member of the police and that he used his reserve force to provide guard duty there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, I'm sorry to say that's the second finally, you told us that you were refused access by the police in Ilidza to the facility. Did you complain? This doesn't appear in your report. Did you tell anybody you had been refused access?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, in the report and when I submitted it to the minister I told him that I couldn't enter and that the chief of the police Mr. Kovac wasn't there. I was certain he would have allowed me to. I told him, minister, you know what the school in Hadzici is like, and I think -- you have a letter of Mr. Mandic to the municipalities in evidence. I suggested to him that it would be a wise thing to do to have those people removed for danger of retaliation by paramilitaries or revenge, and indeed it was followed through later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Avlijas.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Avlijas.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What you said at the end about Vogosca and Brano Vlaco what period did you have in mind when you say you think he had been a policeman?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Before the war he had been a policeman, and at the beginning of the war he was an employee of the police station in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Could the counsel and witness pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you know that he was -- we are being asked to pause. Let me check what's in the transcript. I asked you whether you knew he had been pensioned off before the war.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I hear that for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the local Crisis Staff decided to engage him on these tasks? And I believe we have been discussing the issue of the bunker.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the local Crisis Staff engaged him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I didn't discuss it, but I believe so, because nothing could be done without the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will show you only two documents then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have document -- please bear with me. 1D04-3059, tab 12. Your Honours, we are still awaiting translation of this document, but since it mainly consists of first and last names it won't be difficult to draw inferences. Perhaps the interpreters can follow, and the witness may read out the title of the document. I will do it: "A list of professional employees of the Serb station -- police station in Vogosca," and this is a payroll for May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, have a close look at the list. When you are done with this page, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let us go to the last page of the document then. Have you had occasion to read it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: On this list of employees of the Vogosca police station we do not find Brano Vlaco; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender this document, but it should be MFI'd pending its translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. There are -- I thought that Mr. Cvijetic might be trying to do this when I saw the documents yesterday. There are two things. Firstly, he never asked the witness, for obvious reasons, whether he'd seen it before because I think the answer would have been no. Secondly, and I'm sure this is inadvertent and that Mr. Cvijetic doesn't intend to mislead either the witness or the Court, but tendered as an exhibit, Exhibit P1506, not so long ago by another witness who dealt with the events in Vogosca is a list of the police in Vogosca, active and reserve police, dated the 28th of May, and shown at number 63 of that list is Brano Vlaco, which is why I said yesterday I have not appreciated that there was any dispute, because it went in without objection and without cross-examination that Mr. Vlaco was, in fact, a police officer. So for the -- I don't see how it can go in through that witness, let alone without a translation. But I don't see the purpose either at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The other thing that occurs to me is that apart from the -- what I would call positive document to which Ms. Korner has -- has referred us, I'm not sure what -- even if it had been translated and all of that, the usefulness of this document would be, which is a -- which merely shows the absence of a name. So I suppose an argument could be constructed on that, but on the face of it, I wouldn't have thought it was it relevant or certainly of very much assistance, the mere absence of something on a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the document speaks for itself, and to me it's useful as a reference for -- frame of reference for the questions I'm about to ask the witness. We had a witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I really need to know what the position is. Is the suggestion that's going to be made now, and it's not been made when a witness was here who could have dealt with it, that Mr. Brano Vlaco was not a member of the Vogosca police in May of 1992, and if so, that should be made absolutely clear and should have been made originally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, we agree with the position taken by Ms. Korner on this. Could we have your response to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was used with the witness who had testified before this Trial Chamber, and based on two -- on another two documents, we established -- well, I cannot say it in front of the witness before I show him a document. Three documents have been used from which we concluded what the witness has just said. To my question whether the Crisis Staff was in a position to install him in that position, he answered affirmatively, and I want to show that using three documents which have already been used with witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, before we wander too far -- too far afield from the very narrow issue, the point that Ms. Korner has raised and has asked for an answer, and we agree that she is entitled to press you on this, is that having regard to the evidence that has been led, is it the position of the Defence of Stanisic that Brano Vlaco was not a member of the police at the relevant time? Because as Ms. Korner has said, having regard to the position heretofore taken, they were entitled to continue on the line that this was not in dispute, and we're merely calling on -- on you to -- to answer Ms. Korner's question so we all know where we're going in respect of that narrow issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have just been informed that the document I referred to is also on the 65 ter list. So I'm not talking about a new document, and it has been used with previous witnesses, only it has been marked differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, that is not the question. I'll try again. Is it the position of the Defence of Stanisic that Brano Vlaco was not a police officer in May of 1992 in Vogosca? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. And it follows from everything I have said, and I want to show that using three documents, but I'm not being allowed to. It would be easiest for me to say yes or no. The Crisis Staff appointed him because he retired before the war, and he wasn't an employee of the police station. We even have an exhibit which you admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, you're not being prevented from challenging this if it is, in fact, your case. All we are saying is that for the sake of clarity, having regard to what appeared to be your position, and when I say "appeared," appeared to the Chamber and would have appeared to the Prosecution, before you opened this line of question that you were not making this challenge. Is it your position that you are? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand why it appeared to you that I do not challenge it. Of course I do challenge it. I think it is clear from what has been established through this witness so far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Now we know where you're headed. Please proceed Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just make one point. Firstly, Your Honour, Mr. Cvijetic must stop giving evidence. We've been saying this over and over again saying that the Crisis Staff appointed him. Secondly, if it is their case, as it was, as it now is they say, for obvious reasons that he was not a member of the police, then may I make it clear there should have been cross-examination of the witness who actually dealt with the document which, as I say, shows Mr. Brano Vlaco, number 63, on the list of active and reserve of police officers. And obviously now that we know, and it's been a thing we've been saying all along, it is important that when the Defence have a positive case to put, it should be put properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we believe we've already ruled on this. Their failure to do so would have -- the consequences would be inevitable. So I don't know with respect, Ms. Korner, that you need exercise yourself about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is not activated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So now that we -- now that we understand what your position is, the document would be marked for identification pending its -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have clarified the situation. The list that I have just shown the witness has been admitted as a Prosecution exhibit on the occasion of the examination of a protected witness. I can give the reference numbers. P1504, and there's also P1519. And this is where the situation was clarified. Mr. Brano Vlaco was employed by the police station Vogosca only in November once he was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is complete nonsense. At the moment when Mr. Cvijetic stopped giving evidence, as far as this document is concerned, it's -- if he wants it in, once he's got his translation, although this witness can say absolutely nothing about it, we're not raising an objection. This -- this stream-of-consciousness giving of evidence should stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the ruling of the Chamber is -- by majority is the document may not be admitted even marked for identification through this witness. I am the dissentient in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will show the next document, 1D04-3601. We're also waiting for a translation to be made. Here. It's titled "List of Reserve Police Officers Who Worked for the SJB of Vogosca in May 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, you can read it, and if you have read the first page, let us turn to the second one.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I'm still reading it. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I will put the position of the Defence to you. Mr. Brano Vlaco was not a member of the police station of Vogosca in May 1992. If you remember you said yesterday that he was introduced to you by people of the Crisis Staff and that he was appointed by the Crisis Staff to do these jobs, and you repeated as much today, if I remember well. After what you have seen now, can you confirm your position and the conclusion you drew?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look, I'm sorry. Please -- I'm sorry, Mr. Avlijas. You cannot mislead the Court, Mr. Cvijetic. If you want to put that to him -- sorry. I shouldn't be addressing him directly, Your Honours. Mr. Cvijetic should, if he wants to put this proposition, is obliged to put before him other documents which contradict the position, but he cannot say, "On what you have seen so far, do you change your position that Mr. Vlaco was a police officer," because it's misleading. He must show him document already as I point out Exhibit 1506, dated the 28th of May, Vogosca police station, role of active and reserve police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us show both the Prosecution's and the Defence Exhibit P1504.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It seems to me, Mr. Cvijetic, that you're faced with a -- I don't know if it's an impossible task, but how useful is it going to be to show two contradictory documents to a witness and ask the witness his conclusion? His conclusion's neither here nor there. It's a matter for the Trial Chamber at the end of the day. So is there any point in persisting down this path that you have -- that you are taking?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no contradiction. The document which was admitted is identical to the one I have just -- I have just shown. They are identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is it -- is it documents P1504 or P1506 that we need to look at? I'm unsure about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did say to Mr. Cvijetic 1504. It's 1506, dated the 28th of May. And if one goes to the third page in English, number 63.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all unused microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So then if -- if we have 1504 without that name on it and a 1506 with that name on it, there is the contradiction Judge Hall was referring to, Mr. Cvijetic, not a contradiction between 1504 and the one you failed to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we're in possession of the payrolls for this police station for all months, May, June, July, August, up until November. We are in possession of all those rolls. Of course, this witness -- or they cannot be tendered through this witness. And Mr. Vlaco cannot be found on those rolls. We have settled this with the protected witness, and he said to us when Mr. Brano Vlaco started working at the police station. Therefore, I will limit myself to a specific question with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: How was Mr. Brano Vlaco introduced to you on that day, Mr. Avlijas, as being who and in which position, and who introduced him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: At that meeting where we were, which we attended, Brano Vlaco was one of those present, and it was said that he -- he was in charge of providing security to prisoners of war, and he was wearing a camouflage uniform from which I concluded that he was a police officer. Later on I found out privately that he was a police officer, and I never heard until now that he was -- he retired before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So that camouflage uniform was a police uniform rather than military uniform?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't be sure at the time. People wore all sorts of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last sentence, and Defence counsel and the witness really should not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. Hold on a minute, Mr. Cvijetic, because the transcript reads that the witness's testimony goes as follows: "Later on I found out privately that he was a police officer," and I just wonder if that was what the witness said. Secondly, my question to the witness would be if the witness understood at the time that Mr. Vlaco was representing the SJB in Vogosca. Was that your understanding of -- of the situation when you actually met Mr. Vlaco?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have been mistaken, but that's how I understood it. I must be honest about it. I found out only today that Brano Vlaco retired before the war, but I know that he was saying that he was a police officer at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you -- how did you find out today that Mr. Vlaco was -- was retired before the war? Where did you get that information from today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the -- from Defence counsel, Mr. Cvijetic. He asked me whether I knew that he had retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that's the first time I heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the exact reason why my complaint about the form of questions that are put. It's counsel giving evidence which the witness is accepting when he doesn't know one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's time for a break. May I continue after the break then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Whenever you're ready you may continue, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, yesterday when you spoke about -- about the way Mr. Vlaco was received as a ministry employee, you said that it was all done between the minister and Mr. Vlaco; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So it wasn't between the Ministry of Interior and Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: You're right. There were no memos between them. It was based on the communications between the Vogosca Crisis Staff and the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, on page 15587, when you were asked who attended this meeting in Vogosca and when you were asked who was there representing Vogosca SJB, you said: "I don't remember, but I think there was a young man, blonde, Blagovcanin." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, Blagovcanin, maybe Maksimovic. Maybe there were two of them but I do remember the blonde man, Blagovcanin, but Maksimovic may have been there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you spoke about those two persons being at the meeting on behalf of the Vogosca SJB. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Later on you were asked in what capacity Mr. Vlaco was there, and you said that he introduced himself as chief of security, or head of security, and that's on pages 15588 and 89. You were asked what uniform he wore. You said he had a uniform, and then you said, "I don't remember whether it was a police or military uniform."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you stand by your answer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Fine. Do you know, since you do live in Bijeljina, that the Vogosca Public Security Station included another Mr. Vlaco who has a moustache and who is now an employee of Bijeljina bank who had you -- used to work in the crime prevention department at the SJB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, yeah I know him. He's now Raiffeisen general manager for the branch office in Bijeljina. He was in the police. I don't know that. I cannot respond to that question. I'm not sure whether he had worked in the police or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There is no need. We cleared this through the witness we discussed before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could we -- could we perhaps ask the witness what the first name of this Mr. Vlaco was, if he knows?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You said -- you heard the Judge. Was it the name who had the same name and surname?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Both of them were called Brano. Now, I don't know whether one was Branko or something else, but because this is a diminutive form of this name, Branislav, Branko, everybody gets to be called Brano.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We will not go into that any further, but -- because we discussed this through a witness who -- I won't say his name because he was a protected witness, but who was better familiar with the situation, and also, we will ask for this Brano Vlaco to come as a witness here and we will clarify it once and for all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. All that I want to ask to be clarified, please, is that we appear to have contradictory answers. It was put to him at line 9 that the Vogosca SJB included another Mr. Vlaco who is now an employee of Bijeljina bank, and the answer was: "I know him. He's now a general manager for the Raiffeisen," I think he said, "branch office in Bijeljina. He was in the police. I don't know that. I cannot respond to the question. I'm not sure whether he worked in the police or not." So I'm not clear at the moment. Was the witness saying he doesn't know one way or the other and is merely accepting what Mr. Cvijetic says to him? So perhaps that ought to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you please clarify this.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I know both of these Brano Vlacos. The guy with a moustache, a sort of stocky guy, he's the general manager of the branch office of Raiffeisen bank in Bijeljina. Before that he used to work in the customs administration. Now, whether he had worked for the Vogosca police, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, we'll now discuss the role of the Vogosca Crisis Staff at the meeting. Yesterday, you told us -- at least it was your impression that Mr. Vlaco carried out his tasks according to an order by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: That was my impression. I cannot tell you that for certain, but I could see that in discussions everyone was looking at the president of the Crisis Staff who was presiding the meeting. His name was Mr. Koprivica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did he act in such a manner that one could tell he was under the jurisdiction of the Crisis Staff, that he was responsible to them and so on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: From this point in time I cannot tell you anything more precise. I just told you what I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to have this verified or corrected in the transcript. It's Rajko Koprivica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me show you another document. 1D384, please. Have you had time to read the document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You haven't seen this document before, have you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I see it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As you can see here, the local organs of the municipality of Zvornik are establishing a prison for more than one municipality. There is mention of Bratunac and Skelani. This document, they're basing on their own decision proclaiming the state of war as you can see in the heading, but they also make reference to regulations that can be found in Article 5, the same regulation that you use in decisions establishing prisons. When you came there to visit the prison, did you know who had formed it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I'm seeing this decision for the first time here. From the point of view how it's drafted, it's a nice decision, but at the time in August of 1992 to make such decisions when the Assembly had already ratified the decision on establishment of prisons, I just cannot believe that someone decided to this. This is a completely wilful act. It does not fit into any system. Was it because of the lack of communication or was it just that acted on their own accord? From this vantage point, I can just say that I'm amazed at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, you told us that you can also view this -- these issues from the point of view of a legalist, but viewing the situation realistically, bearing in mind the conditions at the time there, let me put a specific question to you: When we look at the fate of the civilians who went from Ilidza, then to Kula, back to Ilidza and then waited for an exchange, and then also the persons who were waiting for exchange in Kula or in Zvornik, you will agree with me that the three days that you spoke about does not apply to them, and it's impossible to regulate the situation through laws and regulations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I agree. I was speaking for the last three days, and conditions in place, that's something else, but this decision, although it's ridiculous and was contrary to the laws of Republika Srpska, still if this decision saved anyone's life, then it was a good decision. I'm speaking as a human being. I don't want to enter into discussing the legality, the constitutionality of this decision, but if this decision saved lives, I can only say I welcome such decisions. I have no other comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In your report you had stated that the chief of the local police station, Mr. Lokancevic said that they don't know what to do with the people because the other side does not want to have them exchanged. It was not for the first time that you came across such a problem.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I do remember this very professional man, Milorad Lokancevic whom I mentioned very often after the war, I found him in a very difficult situation in Zvornik then, who told me that by taking over the police station -- when he was taking over the police station, he got as heritage, so to speak, or responsibility of 46 or 48 -- 48 or 60 people, maybe, who were grouped according to certain categories, that they are a burden for him because they are in his prison, that he was trying to exchange them, and that he informed also Minister Kalinic, who was the minister of health, who naturally human treatment is something that would fall under the mandate of the ministry of health. So this man was sending lists everywhere to deal with this situation, and then I told him, "Well, give me the list, and I will include that in my report. Let's hope that we can save the people." And I do hope that these people were saved eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You said you believed that they were saved.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, because I didn't get any feedback.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. If we link this up with what you've been told at Ilidza, and let me remind you, you said that they'd also told you they don't know what to do, that they find it a problem and that it's not their jurisdiction and so on, that they don't know what to do.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't told that at Ilidza. I was hold that in Hadzici because the same group of people were then returned to the same location, I think, in September after a failed exchange, to the same place where they had been tortured and humiliated by members of the paramilitaries in the municipality of Hadzici. The police commander was saying, "God, please help me get rid of this burden." I was tasked with providing security for them. Everybody else is on the front line. Somebody has to take care of these people and secure them. There was one detail if you want me to tell you something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It would be interesting to all the participants. After the exchange failed, Amir Masovic was the president of the commission who was with the Muslim population. It was late at night. They could not come back, and the police commander from Hadzici by the name of Brano Mijatovic took Mr. Masovic by the hand, and he took him from Kobiljaca to his apartment in Hadzici which is 15 kilometres away. The Muslims had been tortured and he told him, listen, you can sleep in my apartment. I guarantee for your life. Here's my gun. If something starts happening you can kill me first. And on the next day he returned him to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Amor Masovic later on became rather famous, and I think you were in contact with him.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: And so we co-operated. I was a member of the Republika Srpska Commission for Cooperation, and according to me Mr. Masovic is a highly professional official.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what was the name of the commission that you and Mr. Masovic worked in?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: We co-operated during the war and after the war. I was a member of the commission of the Republika Srpska for missing civilians and fighters of Republika Srpska in the period between 1999 and 2001, and in the course of the war since April 1993, up until 1996, or even 1997, I was a member of the central commission of Republika Srpska for exchange of prisoners of war and the bodies of those killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me just say -- or ask you whether it was your impression that in the police stations where you had found these people, whether people were aware that it's not part of their authority to keep -- or jurisdiction to keep these people but that they don't have any other solution.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I can only speak about Hadzici and Zvornik, but there people were saying, "We don't have any solution. We would like to get rid of this burden. We don't need it, but there's nothing we can do."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Avlijas.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic. I appear on behalf of Stojan Zupljanin. I will have some questions of you in regard to your testimony. The same as with Mr. Cvijetic, since we share the same language, I would kindly ask you to pause, especially in view of the fact that I speak fast. Do break between questions and answers so that we wouldn't have any problems with interpretation. Mr. Avlijas, I wanted to go back to a topic touched upon by Mr. Cvijetic which had to do with the authority of the Crisis Staffs in the territory you visited. When you answered to Mr. Cvijetic's questions, you said, among other things, if I understood correctly, that you could notice that the Crisis Staffs were basically the main and sole authority in those areas, and they expanded their authority so as to include things within their remit which they ordinarily were not supposed to.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, I can't go into the framework of their authority, but I know that nothing could be done without them. For example, in Ilidza, nothing could be done without the Crisis Staff president Mr. Stojicevic's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You were also asked a number of questions about remand prisons or whatever they call them, collection centres for prisoners, depending on what names were used by either of the sides, the Muslim and the Serb. I wanted show you Exhibit P391. You surely know that besides your commission there were -- there was a number of other commissions in the RS which dealt with the situation in individual collection centres. Let me call them that way. This is a report of that kind for Sanski Most, of the SJB in Sanski Most, for the CSB commission. Have a look at paragraph 2 whereby it says: "The Crisis Staff of the municipality ordered the investigation centres to be set up. It made the decision that a prison should be set up in the Betonirka company facilities. It appointed the warden and assistant warden of the prison, who were given personnel for physical security. The personnel consisted of members of the former TO and four or five members of the reserve police force." Mr. Avlijas, it is clear from this that they basically established a prison and organised prison guards following a decision of the Ministry of Justice. Is it not the case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, they basically assumed the authority of the Assembly, because legislation is not used to establish prisons. Hence, I have no comment. This is the first time I see this document, and there's nothing I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And they also organised the prison guards. They established an entire prison, including the security staff.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. They organised the whole thing. Let me have a look further. Formation of collection investigation centre -- centres was ordered by the Crisis Staff. They basically had it all in one, collection centre, investigation prison or remand prison, and a gaol. And they also secured security staff from the TO and the reserve police force without the knowledge of the district court which otherwise, under the law, is duty-bound to supervise remand prisons and other such facilities under the Law on Criminal Procedure. This was in contravention with the instruction of the organisation of prisons under the law, and they basically bypassed any and all decisions of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You are also familiar with the fact that certain representatives of Crisis Staffs even assumed the right to pardon prisoners.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, I had such an example in Foca. I went there in December 1992. Since I was in charge of misdemeanour courts, I went to the court and it was presided over by a female judge, Mandic. What she told me was this: "Just imagine, learned friend, we had the Crisis Staff president pardoning convicts." I immediately advised the minister. And it was a terrible thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, you were shown an exhibit by the Prosecutor, which is P1635.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I have already commented upon this report. Actually, I testified in full about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, it has to do with a meeting: Mr. Milan Trbojevic who was deputy prime minister was in charge of control and co-ordination between the two ministries, the ministry of the interior and of justice; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: He was the deputy prime minister in charge of internal policy, and we all know what that encompasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you look closely at the report, especially the last sentence of the first paragraph when those in attendance are mentioned, it is stated they held a meeting on the topic of situation and problems of prisoners camps in this area. That was the point of the meeting, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, but it also touched upon the organisation of military courts, co-operation with the ICRC, and other topical issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radic informed those in attendance of the number of prisoner centres and the problems they had with such facilities, and we can also find it in your report.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see in your report, and as far as I can understand your testimony, you were then told that such prisoners centres in Omarska and Keraterm were disbanded, and as far as I can see here, there was still a collection centre in Trnopolje which was not a full camp.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. It was commented upon. We were informed of it at the meeting. We were told that it was a town hall and a school where those people gathered by themselves. They cooked there, and some of them awaited their departure to leave for some other country or to simply leave the territory of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you say as much in your report by saying: "Muslims are accommodated in those facilities, who took shelter there in fear of revenge by paramilitaries." Those facilities have a free entry and exit policy. What you were basically told is that people came there voluntarily, that no one was forced to be there.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, that's the extent of the information I received at the meeting. So it was indirect information. I did not personally go to these locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go to page 2 of the document. The last paragraph. It has to do with what you have just said. It says: "Following this joint meeting, a meeting was held especially with presidents of the courts and prosecutors, as well as representatives of the Ministry of Defence. The topic of the meeting was the organisation and functioning of the Military Court and military prosecutor's offices, which do not function at all in the Krajina." One of the problems, we did not touch upon your remit directly, was that the military judiciary as well as parts of the civilian judiciary did not function properly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. It is. The number of crimes under the then law committed by soldiers was great. They were all seen as soldiers. Under the law if a member of the armed forces commits a crime, it falls under the jurisdiction of the Military Prosecutor's Office and the military court, and there were -- this was a cause of frequent conflicts and misunderstandings between the civilian and military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the gist of it is that the perpetrators were not adequately prosecuted, which caused a lot of problems in terms of public law and order.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, yes. It had an impact on the environment as a whole in those area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You discussed this with the Prosecutor already. At the meeting, a question of the murder of several people at Koricanske Stijene was raised.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. The late Dr. Radic, Banja Luka mayor, insisted on receiving some sort of explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Zupljanin addressed the issue, you said that when he referred to the work of the police he said that the Banja Luka police that they're part of the work and it was up to the prosecution now, the prosecutor's office, and that they should be asked about the fate of the case and why there was nothing being done about it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. There was arguments exchanged. People mentioned how many innocent people were killed for no reason. This was a rampage, and this was -- that's how the Banja Luka mayor characterised it. He insisted on clearing up the situation. I saw Stojan Zupljanin for the first time then when he said that he had established a team which visited this scene to gather information. I cannot recall everything exactly, but I think the army offered rescue teams to go down the gorge in order to reach the bodies, which was otherwise impossible to do. He said he could do his utmost and submitted a criminal report to the prosecutor's office, and then he put a question to Mr. Puvacic who was the basic prosecutor as to what he intended to do, because he said that the ball was in his court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the suspects or potential perpetrators of the crime, it was said that the crime was committed by those who were escorting the convoy.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, let's not reinvent the wheel here. The entire RS knows that it was done by members of the SJB in Prijedor, commanded by Simo Drljaca. That was no secret. I believe even some names of those in the escort were circulated, and Mr. Simo Drljaca said that some of the policemen were on the run because he was directly asked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know those suspected of having committed that crime were transferred to Han Pijesak in order to prevent them -- their arrest?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm not familiar with this fact. I hear of it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: A part of my question is missing. I said that in the meantime, they had joined the army of the of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of it. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that was when Mr. Zupljanin also said to all those present about the identification and the apprehension of the suspected perpetrators, that Mr. Drljaca or -- or, rather, he singled out Mr. Drljaca and said that they were on the run.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Not only Mr. Zupljanin. Everybody mentioned Simo Drljaca, because they were supposed to go to Travnik, and there was an escort, there was a convoy of buses, and it was within the remit of the public security at Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his answer, and slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the interpreters ask that you repeat the last part of your answer and that you attempt to speak more slowly in your answers. It is hard to interpreter correctly when the speakers are speaking too fast. Thank you very much, sir. Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is no secret at all, and it was known on that day at the meeting. The entire Krajina and all of the RS knew that the police station, or SJB, I'm not sure of the exact name at the time, was in charge of escorting a civilian convoy, a convoy of civilian population, I think predominantly of Muslim ethnicity, I don't know whether there were any Croats among them, from Prijedor, because they were inhabitants of Prijedor, to Travnik, which was under the control of the opposite side. And everybody present at the meeting knew that the massacre, the crime, had been committed by members of the Prijedor Police Station, the chief of which was Simo Drljaca. Only it wasn't known whether it was active-duty police officers or reserve police officers who had done it. There was no doubt about whether or not the crime had been committed or not.
