Everything was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It was at that meeting that Mr. Drljaca said that they were on the run, that they were impossible to find, and that he could do nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It was an ugly story, but there was no normal reaction to such criticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to correct the transcript. You actually said that it's not appropriate to speak about dead people.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. I apologise. If I may comment. Imagine an official meeting in Banja Luka, the most high-ranking officials of the entire Krajina, and everybody speaks about a terrible crime without any self-criticism and with -- and there's no responsibility. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And not only from the Krajina but also the prime minister and the minister of justice and generals. Obviously, nobody had enough authority over Simo Drljaca; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. That's my conclusion, because if it had been a well-functioning state, Simo Drljaca should have been locked up. If there is command responsibility in a well-functioning state, then there can be no discussion about it. A hundred and fifty or 200 people were killed. The chief of police is at -- at a meeting, and the police officers who had committed a crime were on the run. I mean, what can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, you said that after that you attended another meeting at Prijedor, and it had to do with Trnopolje also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show the witness Exhibit P393.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is your report from October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's show the witness item 4. That's on page 3 of the Serbian. Actually, the pagination shows 2, but it's item 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Here you speak about the situation in Prijedor, and you mention Trnopolje are, and it says: "The former collection centre at Trnopolje was closed down following the agreement. However, because of irresponsible people in Prijedor who launched the false information among the Muslim population --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's turn the page in Serbian. The page in English should stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: "-- that the only way to leave this town is to gather at the Trnopolje collection centre and that the organisation will be by the International Red Cross exclusively." And you go on to speak about the meeting in Prijedor where a representative of the ICRC appear -- appeared. Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Dr. Beat. I co-operated very well with him, and it was with him that I visited Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there was no collection centre in Trnopolje where people gathered spontaneously. It was also confirmed by Dr. Beat.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It was stated at the meeting, because when we went to Trnopolje, there was nothing left. If I may comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: At that meeting, we were informed that somebody had placed that story on purpose. I cannot prove that, however, who was -- who was behind that, only to have the people gather at the collection centre to enable others to loot their homes. That was the basic reason. That's what was said to us at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let us display page 4 of this document. You were saying earlier, answering the Prosecutor's question, from whom you had got that information, from officers of military security regarding Sanski Most, but you also mentioned Kotor Varos. I believe that you made a mistake there.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Teslic, yes. It was Teslic, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So this part that you wrote in the report refers to Teslic rather than Kotor Varos; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. We couldn't access the area to the right of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you learned from the officers that there was a POW camp controlled by the Serb military.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they told me so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Pribinic mean anything to you? Does it sound familiar, speaking about Teslic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. I hear it for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking about Manjaca which was discussed here, there is no doubt that it was a POW camp controlled and commanded by the army; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. It was under the exclusive authority of the army. They provided security. It so happened that I was involved in the exchange that I conducted with the late Ivo Rosic and Dr. Branko Dokic with the Croatian side from Mostar for Croatian and Serb civilians at Pakovo near Sibenik. And when I visited Manjaca, a major was the commander of the camp. I forget his name. It was only the army that had authority over that camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Avlijas. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were -- sorry. You were asked a moment ago by Mr. Krgovic about Mr. Drljaca. It was put to you that nobody had enough authority over Mr. Drljaca, and you said: "Yes, that's your conclusion, because had it been a well-functioning state, Simo Drljaca should have been locked up." At that meeting there was a representative of the Banja Luka Corps you told us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stojan Zupljanin was there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, the minister of defence was there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, the deputy prime minister was there.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Any one of those people had the authority, did they not, had they wished to exercise it, to ensure that Mr. Drljaca was arrested?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I phrased it correctly, "in a well-functioning state," but nobody could harm Simo Drljaca. He was the sheriff of Prijedor. And I can say openly I believe that I told the investigators when they asked me about staffing and dealing with personnel issues, it was the SDS that was consulted about everything, and I asked whether -- or, rather, I was asked whether a minister could appoint anyone, and I answered that he could when he got approval to do so. And I know that everybody was -- had a hard time replacing Simo Drljaca. Well, from the perspective of a well-functioning state this may seem odd, but -- and I agree that he shouldn't have been at the meeting at all, that he should have been in gaol if he was responsible for the death of 200 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know how large the Banja Luka Corps was, which was then the 1st Krajina Corps? How many people it had.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I don't know, believe me. I know that it was a large unit, the biggest corps, bearing in mind the area of responsibility of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were Special Police available to Mr. Zupljanin in Banja Luka, a group of Special Police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know about that. I'm not competent to speak about the power of individual MUP officials. I don't know what was within whose authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But from what you're saying, there was sufficient manpower to arrest Simo Drljaca had anybody wanted to do it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I cannot comment that. Every Crisis Staff and every region was actually a state within a state, and what I'm about to say is my opinion, so for what it's worth: Simo Drljaca was the untouchable boss of Prijedor and its surroundings. In the eyes of some shady people, he was their idol, and it was carefully considered what to do when it came to replacing people, and I believe it was the SDS's fault that they didn't allow the professionals to do their work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say that he was the untouchable boss. Is that because nobody wanted to touch him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Believe me, I cannot answer this question. I told you that those were my opinions and my observations from going to the field every day. I wasn't in the political structures. I didn't decide about anything. I never joined any party, and that's why I was left without a job. I was fired from my job in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told, I think it was Mr. Cvijetic, that you were appointed to the Commission of Exchange in 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was Simo Drljaca appointed to that commission as well?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes. One of the members of the commission was Simo Drljaca as representative of the MUP, because they tried to get rid of him and appointed him to such a commission dealing with these humanitarian issues, which is -- which I cannot understand. And he had in the meantime been relieved of his position in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So he could be relieved of his position in Prijedor. He could be removed from Prijedor and sent to the commission, but he couldn't be arrested.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I cannot answer this comment of yours. What I'm saying is had the state been functioning properly, he should have been arrested. Why wasn't he arrested? I don't know. I'm answering you in such a way as to explain what I would have done had I been in power, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He was appointed to the commission as the representative of the MUP. Do you know who was responsible in the MUP for making that appointment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: The minister, Ratko Adzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You also were shown the document from Sanski Most, the report of the SJB in August, which showed that instead of the four prisoners that you had been told about, there were some 1.655 prisoners in Sanski Most. Did anybody every say -- tell you that before you saw that report today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who was that? And when?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: In. No, I said yes, yes I can answer. This is an information that was made in August, this information from Sanski Most, and I was there in October. I know that all the prisoners from that part of Krajina were driven away, that they were at Manjaca. So if there was more than a thousand of them, that they were transferred to Manjaca. One can find documentation confirming that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm sorry, what you put into the report that you delivered to Mr. Mandic -- and perhaps we'd better have it up again. It's document -- so sorry.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: In October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. I've lost the exhibit number again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's P393. Can we go, please, to the part of Sanski Most, which is on the fifth page in English and the fourth in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What you wrote down was: "The information that there is a camp in Sanski Most is not correct. In that area, only four people were taken prisoner and transferred to Manjaca during combat activities." Now, had you been given information before, and that's why you were asking about Sanski Most, that considerably more people had been captured and taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, the people who were detained in Sanski Most in August, who were in Keraterm, who were in other camps such as Omarska, and this whole stretch between Banja Luka and Prijedor, they were all transferred, three or 4.000 of them were transferred to Manjaca. At the time of drafting of this report of mine which was in October, the officer from the corps informed me that there were additional four persons who had been captured and transferred to Manjaca. This is what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. So what you intended to convey by this, do I understand this correctly, was that since August, there were only four other people who had been taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Between the drafting of my report -- or during the time while I was drafting my report, he told me that during that period four other prisoners were captured because there may have been fighting there, and that all four of them were transferred in the meantime to Manjaca in addition to all the others that had been transferred earlier. Of course, those who were still alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see, would you -- if you read that report, it sounds as though throughout the whole period only four people had been taken prisoner. Would you -- would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No, I cannot accept that. I was drafting a report about the situation at the time and not about how many people were captured throughout the war. I was told to go and check how many people were there captured. I went to Vlasenica, Zvornik, and all the other locations that are mentioned here in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much, Mr. Avlijas. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, thank you very much for your assistance to the Tribunal. You are now released, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, where are you in terms of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, never have I seen a more topsy-turvy set of days, because the estimate for this witness was something in the region of four hours cross-examination, which is why we were so anxious to conclude him. In fact, we can, if Your Honours rise, we can start the next witness at 12.15, which witness is -- ST-251. And he has protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We are advised that he won't be available until 12 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: He wouldn't be in the room until 12.15 so we're probably looking at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do we -- once we start him, where do we go? Do we still need the reserved session this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Obviously, Your Honours, it would help, because he's supposed to be a short -- Your Honour, this witness is short, and if Your Honours were to sit a little bit into the afternoon, we could probably complete him today. In fact, we may be able to complete him. I don't think Mr. Hannis, who is calling the witness, intends to be more than about 30 minutes with him. I'm told 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we reconvene at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just add something. We only now received the documents concerning the coming witness. He was scheduled to testify on Monday. We certainly cannot cross-examine the witness at the moment regardless of the fact it's going to be a short witness and he's going to be discussing very limited set of facts in relation to adjudicated facts. If we could cross-examine this witness on Monday maybe. The Prosecution can do their direct now and then we would like to do the cross-examination on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After all the topsy-turviness concerning the previous witness, we believed that this following witness would start on Monday. I don't even have the documentation necessary to go through, but maybe we could compensate for the time we've spent yesterday by doing this on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I've heard what Mr. Krgovic and Mr. Cvijetic have said, but I thought the switching this witness on Monday only occurred in the very latest schedule that came out this morning, so I'm surprised that each of them has indicated that they're embarrassed by having to cross-examine him today. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, also I don't -- I'm told that we applied for protective measures which I don't think have been objected to, but I don't think we've had a formal decision granting them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What are you asking?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The documents are only photographs and maps, no other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this witness wasn't scheduled after of Mr. Avlijas. It was Mr. ST-227. That's the problem that we're facing. We received the proofing notes and other documents only ten minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, in the plan that I have for this week, clearly Witness ST-251 was scheduled to begin his testimony today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm told we'll offer them either. They can have 227 or 251. Both of them are here and both are ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So with which of them would you prefer to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We would prefer to call 251 because he is the one who has problems with his job and would like to get back if at all possible. And is also shorter than the other witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsels, I think Witness 251 is -- is one of the adjudicated fact witnesses. Is that correct, Mrs. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And so the testimony that he is going to offer is going to be very, very limited, and I wonder if we postpone him until, say, 1.00 or even 1.30, if that would give you enough time to -- to just flip through his -- his documents and then be ready for his cross-examination. I think it would be helpful if we could finish him off by the end of this day's session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. Cross-examination of the witnesses that are here for adjudicated facts should be very short providing the Prosecutor's Office keeps to that topic, maybe five or so minutes. What Judge Harhoff suggested would be fine. If we start at 1.30, by quarter to 2.00 we would all be finished. Mr. Cvijetic I believe will not have any questions in cross-examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't follow that. Your Honours, that can't be right. If we adjourn until 1.30 and there's examination-in-chief, cross-examination will not be completed by quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I was saying I was in favour of this first version that was presented by Judge Harhoff, namely that we start at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the -- so before we adjourn, I just want the -- to be clear as to what we're doing, and I invite the court officer to correct me if I get it wrong. We rise now. We resume at 1.00, and we sit until, at the very latest, 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So the -- again, we appreciate the co-operation of the accused in this regard and those who have the custody of them would have noted what I would have said in terms of time. So we resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Firstly, for the record, please note that we reconvene for this final session of today under Rule 15 bis. Secondly, the Trial Chamber affirms in accordance with the Rules the protective measures that have previously been afforded to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In conjunction with that, his -- his pseudonym that he had from the previous case was a case specific number, and our request was that he assigned the number ST-251 for our purposes in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So could the witness be invited to make the solemn declaration first of all, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may be seated. The -- I remind you that the solemn declaration that you have made imposes a new obligation to give truthful testimony subject to the penalties that the Tribunal is empowered to impose for giving false or misleading testimony. The first thing I would invite the Prosecution to do is to -- you have the pseudonym sheet, I suppose. You're going to be handed a sheet of paper. If you would confirm that that correctly indicates your name and other relevant particulars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And if you're so satisfied, we would invite you to sign that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's admitted as an exhibit under seal. And I would remind you that the purpose of that is because exceptionally, the Chamber has afforded you certain protective measures of a pseudonym, and therefore in the course of your testimony you would be referred to either by that pseudonym or by -- just referred to as "Mr. Witness" to facilitate your testimony. I needn't explain to you. As I said, this is an exceptional measure, because as far as possible the proceedings of the Tribunal are held entirely in public, but for reasons which would have been fully canvassed when you last appeared before the Tribunal, the -- you have been granted the modified protection -- protective measures of a pseudonym and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Facial distortion, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And facial distortion. Thank you, Mr. Hannis. The -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, I would like to mention that the pseudonym sheet for Witness ST-251 shall be given Exhibit P01636. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. The -- you have been called to give testimony within a very limited scope today, and therefore we fully expect that you -- your testimony would be completed before we rise for the day in a little over an hour. So the -- with that I would invite Mr. Hannis to begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. This witness has been called particularly to address adjudicated fact 1145. However, he -- I do need to reference another adjudicated fact connected with him, which is 1138. That was accepted by the Trial Chamber in its entirety, but just in setting the background for this witness, I will make reference to it so you know who he is and where he's from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us where you were living in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: In Sanski Most, in the village of Hrustovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall when the war broke out in the vicinity of your village, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what month that was?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: It was end of May 1992, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did you do when the fighting began in your village in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: I was not employed. I wasn't doing anything special. I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you -- did you remain in the village throughout the fighting or did you leave the area?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: The village of Hrustovo I left before the fighting that took place in Hrustovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: To the neighbouring village, Klijevci, where my grandmother lived, and my uncle as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's also the municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to tell you about an adjudicated fact that we have in this case and ask you just a couple of questions about this. Around -- this is adjudicated fact 1138, for the record, which says on or around 27 June 1992, local Serb reservists in olive-grey uniforms arrived at the Muslim hamlet of Kenjari. It goes on to say that 20 Muslim men were arrested and interrogated, that Vlado Vrkes, president of the Sanski Most SDS assured them they had nothing to fear. They were led by Serb soldiers to a house in the hamlet of Blazevici, pardon my pronunciation. Soldiers threw explosives into the house and then opened fire with rifles on those trying to escape. The bodies of the dead were taken back into the house and the house was set on fire. Do you know who those 20 men were? I'm not asking you to name them right now, just did you know those men?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Yes, I knew those men. They were inhabitants of hamlets of Kenjari and Zukici, and one or two men whose houses were a bit remote, but all of them were part of Klijevci.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you one of that group of 20 men?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What happened to the other 19?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: They were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did you -- well, what did you do when you apparently survived and managed to get away? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: From the house in Blazevici I went to Hrustovo to my hamlet where I lived. I decided to go home and see what the situation was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't think we asked you before, but your ethnicity is?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: I am a Bosniak, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How long did you -- well, that was -- I'm sorry. That event was on or about the 27th of June. How long --

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Yes. That was a month after Hrustovo was taken by the Serbian forces and after they'd done what they'd done there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to go to the village of Tomina in Sanski Most municipality?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Yes. After I reached my home and saw what it looked like, that there were no inhabitants there, I headed towards the village of Tomina. While I was still in Zukici or Kenjari, I knew that inhabitants of Hrustovo and Vrhpolje were driven away to a place called Tominska Palanka, which is part of Tomina where exclusively Muslims resided.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long did you remain at Tomina before you went or were taken somewhere else, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: I think four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What happened at the end of those four days?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: So on the fourth day, in the morning, we heard a police car. Through a bullhorn they were calling all the inhabitants of Hrustovo, Vrhpolje and Kamicak to come out to the main road between Sanski Most and Kljuc. So they asked us to appear there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you do that, and, if so, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Yes. We all came out, all of us, from Hrustovo, Vrhpolje, and Kamicak. We all went to the main road and there we were put into buses and then we headed towards Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was -- who was doing that? Who was gathering you together and putting you on the buses and sending you to Sanski Most? What people were doing that?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: The police and the Serbian Army. I remember well that the driver of this Golf vehicle was a teacher at high school in Sanski Most. His surname was Banjac, but I don't remember or don't know his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the police -- you said the Serbian Army. Were the police also Serbian?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Yes. I said both the police and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: The buses brought us to a -- a hole in Sanski Most. Actually, it was located on the road between Sanski Most and Bosanska Krupa, not far from Sanski Most. It was an industrial area, and there was this large hole there, and that's where they got us out of the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of this hall in the industrial area?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: I later found out it was called Krings, most probably a company from Austria making cables was located there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at Krings in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: We had to enter it and wait. We simply didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had you been told why you were taken to this location?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who at that end in Sanski Most at Krings was taking you off the bus and placing you inside the building?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: The escort was provided by the Serbian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from that point how long did you stay at Krings before you were eventually released?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: I think it was a month, give or take a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you first a -- a map that is exhibit P411.37. This is a -- this is a document that's already in evidence, sir, and it will be up on your screen in a moment. I just want to ask you if you can confirm something for me. While it's coming up, I can tell you it's a map of Sanski Most town area with some photographs on the side. And on the map, on the left side, near the middle you'll see the number 4 and the word "Krings" under it. Does that accurately show the relative location of where Krings was in Sanski Most town?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the road we see running above Krings, do you know where that road went to? The one that runs from left to right above Krings.

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: The road goes from Sanski Most, Lucica Palanka, towards Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like next to show you Exhibit P414. Can you tell us what that's a picture of?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Am I allowed to stand up, because I have a reflection on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Yes. That's the industrial hall where we were held. But it's been refurbished and there seem to be some -- there seems to be some machinery there which wasn't there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And one more photo. If I could show you P415. And again if you need to stand up or you need a hard copy of the photo, let me know.

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: I can see much better from here. This is most likely the hall, but there were no trucks or material inside when we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time you were placed in the Krings Hall, what was inside, if anything?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: The hall was almost empty. You could see old pallets and parts of machinery that had been left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many of you were taken to Krings Hall when you first went there? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: The first day when we arrived there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: The hall was quite full, so I think between 6 and 700 people. There were children and women there as well as the elderly and middle-aged men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you first arrived there was there anybody already there or was it empty?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: When we arrived, the hall was empty, but the buses kept coming, as well as trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the 6 to 700 people that you mentioned, what was -- the 600 to 700 people you mentioned, what was the ethnicity of all of you?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Muslim. Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where were those people from? I know you were brought from Tomina, but were all these people from Tomina or other villages in Sanski Most municipality?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: The people who were there were from the villages of Hrustovo, Vrhpolje, and Kamicak who had been driven out from places such as Tomina, Caplje, et cetera. We were all put together in the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you told us before that I think you remained there for a month. What about the women and children that were first detained with you? How long did they stay?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: We spent the first night there together, and early the next morning some soldiers arrived who said that the women, children, and those over 60, as well as the handicapped, were to leave on board buses and trucks. They were taken elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Approximately how many of you men, then, of I guess ages between 16 and 60 remained behind?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: I can't say precisely. I think between a hundred and a hundred and fifty. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was guarding you while you were there at Krings?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: We were locked inside the hall, and outside there were Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you why you were being detained during your month there?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: No. Nobody told us anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long did the Serb soldiers continue to guard you during your month there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, an objection to this line of questioning. Any further questions go beyond the testimony of this witness and the purpose of his testimony, which is the adjudicated fact regarding the humanitarian conditions and the location where the witness was held. If one bears in mind this Trial Chamber's decision by which it is stated that testimony of this time needs -- of this kind needs to be focused exclusively on the adjudicated fact for which the witness is being called and possibly to testify to a certain extent on the background. In any case, this line of questioning goes well beyond the context itself and the adjudicated fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I -- if I may. I disagree. I'm laying the foundation to get to precisely the portion of the adjudicated fact that was stricken by the Trial Chamber in its decision, the last sentence in fact 1145, and I have to lay some foundation before I can ask him the specific questions related to that. If I may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, but bear in mind what Mr. Krgovic has correctly stated about the circumscription concerning your questions and come rapidly to the adjudicated fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you -- did you recall my last question? How long did Serb soldiers continue to guard you from your first day there? Were they guarding you for the entire month?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: No they were there for a week perhaps. After that I believe the reserve police from Sanski Most came, although I'm not certain whether they were reserve policemen or active-duty policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It was not mentioned in the summary of this witness or in adjudicated fact the role of the police in the specific adjudicated fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness was listed as the witness to call to address the adjudicated fact 1145 and that portion which was stricken out. I see no way the Defence could not see that he was going to testify about police involvement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees. Please move on, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would indicate that the 65 ter summary indicates that about 15 days -- after about 15 days, the police took over guard duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there a difference in how you were treated after the police began guarding you as compared to how you were treated by the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Yes. During the time when we were guarded by the soldiers, our relatives, parents, or our wives could bring food to us, to the hall, and we could talk to them. However, when the police arrived, our relatives could no longer enter, and they started beating us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who started beating you?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: The policemen who stood guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Of the police who were guarding you during those last couple of weeks that you were at Krings, did you know or recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Yes. I knew a young guy of my age. We attended school together. We weren't in the same class, but we frequently ran into each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall his name or nickname?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: I think his first name is Srecko, and I'm not sure whether that's actually his first name or his nickname. In any case, he lived in the building across the street from the high school centre in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And anyone else that you recognised among the policemen?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: I was only 20 then, and I didn't know many people in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While you were detained there, were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Towards the end of the month I spent there, we were interrogated for a day by the policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the policemen that interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: During the interrogation, some other policemen came who I believe were more senior to those reserve of policemen. I knew one of them from before since my uncle had been a policeman in Sanski Most. Occasionally would I see that particular policeman whose wife was a secretary in the high school. I think he was -- his name was Drago Macura, although I believe Macura is only his nickname. In any case, he was strongly built and had a moustache. I remember him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned while the police were guarding you that there were some beatings. How were these beatings carried out? What were they done with, if you know. Was it feet and hands, or were any instruments used?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Yes. I remember they used batons a lot, rifle butts, fists, feet, a rod that is otherwise used to clean a rifle. They also used that to hit us with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know a man named Ejub Masic?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Ejub Masic. I didn't know that man. In any case, he was brought in front of the hall one evening where he was beaten up. Later on, they threw him inside. The next day, the next morning, when we awoke he was dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say they threw him inside, who -- who was guarding you at the time this event occurred?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Well, he was brought in front of the hall, beaten up and then thrown inside the hall, and at that point in time we were guarded by the policemen. The army had already gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see who did the actual beating in front of the hall?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: I couldn't see that since the hall was closed and it was dark outside. Even when he was thrown inside, I couldn't make out who threw him in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after your month of being detained at Krings, what happened to you? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Before my release, I had been interrogated by those higher-ranking policemen, as I said. They wanted to know where I had been, where I had weapons, what I did. And after that, all those 40 men who had been there since day one were released. I think everyone was released, because I was among the last ones to be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had you had any weapons or engaged in any fighting?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I don't have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the Defence begins its cross-examination, I just have one question for the witness relating to the interrogations that you mentioned, and my question is if any beatings or maltreatment took place during the interrogations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so. When I was being interrogated, the policeman I mentioned, Drago Macura, kept moving from one room to the next. There were several policemen interrogating us at the same time. He entered our room and asked the policeman interrogating me whether he needed help when interrogating. But whoever -- it implied beating me up, because he was holding a bat. The policeman responded negatively, and at that time he didn't hit me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But did you hear any beatings going on in the adjacent rooms where other interrogations were made or were going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I returned to the hall after the interrogation, we talked about it, and some people told me that they were well beaten up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic and I appear on behalf of Stojan Zupljanin. I will have some questions of you regarding your testimony. Just one or two words of warning. Since we understand each other and use the same language, please wait for a moment or two before answering so as to avoid any overlap. Another thing, when I'm done putting my questions, please look at the red light on my microphone, because you enjoy certain protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have voice and face distortion? Very well then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I just didn't want anyone else to hear your voice, but you can disregard this remark. I would start from the end of the Prosecutor's questions. If I understood well, in the hall at Krings itself, there were no interrogations. You were taken outside to be interrogated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Yes. It took place in a small building in front of the hall where there used to be offices of those who were in charge of the company. On the photographs I was shown, that building is no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That is how I understood it. So in the hall itself there was no interrogation. You were taken outside into that building where the policeman interrogated you, following which you were returned into the hall; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: They wanted to know about your movements in the past few months and whether you had any weapons, as well as whether you took part in combat or in any way assisted or abetted this organisation of support offered by the Muslim population in that area.

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Yes. They wanted to know if I knew who had weapons and who fired them. Since I had learned earlier on that some people from my village had been killed, I simply told them that those were the people who had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I looked at your statement where I believe you mention your personal weapons. I believe you said that you had a handgun which you handed over to your neighbour when there was a request to hand over weapons. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That is actually your testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I have a precise reference, because I think his testimony was that his relative had a gun and he passed that gun to someone else. So can we have a page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 8054.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you said that it was your father, if I understand the testimony well, had a weapon that was given to a neighbour who in turn handed it over to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Are you referring to my previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: The weapon was given to him, and the man took it to Klijevci, the neighbouring village where the Serb army was, and that man never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were you also asked about that particular piece? I suppose your father had a licence for it?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: It was not a licensed gun. I don't know whether they aimed for that or whether they wanted to know whether I had been in the armed forces or something else. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In response to my learned friend's question about when you arrived in the Krings Hall, I -- you said something that I wanted to link to a certain document. I would like to show you the document indicating the date as of which the centre existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P391 shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe you have had occasion to see this document before, not even in proofing. In any case, this was an SJB Sanski Most report on the existence of such centres following a request of the CSB in Banja Luka. It is stated therein that there had been a centre in the gym which was then emptied and that as of the 1st of August, 1992, the gym is empty, and another collection centre was established in the hall of the Krings factory. So my question to you is whether before arriving at Krings you had been in this gym, or did you come to Krings from your place of residence?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Do you mean whether I was in the gym?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the date when you were released from Krings?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: I think it's in my statement. I can't recall the date now, but I think I left Sanski Most on the 18th of August, and before leaving Sanski Most I spent some two weeks with a relative there. So I'd say it was in early August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Another question. If you look at the next paragraph of this document, it is stated that the prison was established as well as a warden appointed, and that the staff came from the reserve police force and the TO. Do you know of any such warden at the Krings?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Yes. It was a young policeman. When the police arrived as opposed to the other policeman, he had a full police uniform, a fatigue, a camouflage police uniform, actually. I think he mentioned his first and last name, but it escapes me now. He was a handsome guy, dark haired, and I believe he said he had worked in the prison in Bosanska Gradiska or in Bosanska Gradiska itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the prison there?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he worked in the prison, but I think by occupation he was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the facility where you were held, please look at the next page of this document. Have a look at the fourth paragraph from the top. The report describes the conditions at Krings.

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: The fourth paragraph? Can you please be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The fourth paragraph from the top. It begins with "The accommodation of all persons -- all persons were quartered in the solidly built facilities of the sports hall." Yes. There is a mention made of the conditions. It is said that the prisoners were given blankets and something to lie on, as well as other things brought by their families.

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: At the beginning when we arrived there, there was nothing in the hall. There were only pallets which we put on the floor so as not to sleep on the concrete floor. Later on our mothers and families brought some blankets or Styrofoam sheets, but in any case, there were no amenities that could be used for sleeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it goes on in the following paragraph where we see about the gymnasium and Krings, that food was provided by the relatives of the detained.

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: While I was there, my mother fed me. I didn't receive anything from the Red Cross. However, there were many more people, and I don't know whether they got anything from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph says: "During their stay, persons in the collection and investigation centre received adequate medical care from the Sanski Most health centre, the personnel of which visited the prisoners and offered essential health care services." Where you seen by a doctor or a nurse from those facilities?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Let me give you an example. There was a Muslim detained with us. I believe his name was Enes Karabeg. He was a doctor by profession. He still works there as a doctor today. There was a man who was in great pain, because while he was asleep some bug entered his ear, and then he banged on the door to call the guards because he wanted somebody to remove that bug because he was in great pain. They took him away, and later on it was all right. But we weren't visited inside by any medical personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question: Answering the question of the Prosecutor, you mentioned that man who was brought to your hall and died on the next day. You said to the Prosecutor that you didn't see him being beaten up or who beat him. You only saw him when he was brought inside.

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: He was beaten just outside the hall. We could hear the beating and those who mistreated him swearing and him giving cries of pain. However, I didn't see who brought him in because it was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But he was not one of those who were detained with you in that same hall?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: From before, no. He was brought on that evening, and he died before the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, after the interrogation, when you said that you had nothing to do with any military activity you were released; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Yes. After the interrogation, I received a letter of release from that facility, and that made it possible for me to leave and go to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anything in redirect, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just a few if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Regarding the man who was beaten outside and who later died, did the entire beating take place outside the hall?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned the interrogations. How many times or days were you interrogated during your 30 days of detention in Krings?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: I was interrogated on one day for about 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who -- who took you to and from Krings when you were taken to the interrogation office?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Then they were all police officers. There was no more army around. They were the guards and also the ones who came. They must have been inspectors or I don't know what. They also interrogated us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how far were those offices where the interrogations were done from where you were detained? Were those offices on the same grounds or premises as the big building we saw in the picture?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: The small building was some 10 to 15 metres away from the hall, but it was part of the overall facility of the whole compound. There were offices in there, so I suppose it was used for the administration, but it was only some 10 to 15 metres away, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And lastly, the man who was beaten and thrown in and then dead the next morning, did anyone ask for medical treatment for him during the night, do you know?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: No one of us did because we didn't dare.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: ST-251
utterances.text: Because everybody was afraid for themselves. Nobody expected him to die. We thought that he would recover.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Witness, this is the end of your testimony. You're now released. We wish you a safe journey home, and the Chamber records its appreciation for your coming to give evidence and notes the suffering that -- that you experienced at the time, and we empathise with you. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hannis, that is it for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. I think we have another witness, but I don't know that it makes sense to try and start him and do 20 minutes. I think it would be better just to start first thing Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So we'll -- the witness may be escorted from the room, and then we'll properly take the adjournment in open court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. If you could assist in raising the shutters. Thank you. So we take the adjournment and resume at 9.00 on Monday morning. I trust everyone has a safe weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th day of October, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.09 p.m.
